==Problem==

How many three-digit positive integers have an odd number of even digits?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }150\qquad\textbf{(B) }250\qquad\textbf{(C) }350\qquad\textbf{(D) }450\qquad\textbf{(E) }550</imath>

==Solution 1==
We use simple case work to solve this problem.

Case 1: even, even, even = <imath>4 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 = 100</imath>

Case 2: even, odd, odd = <imath>4 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 = 100</imath>

Case 3: odd, even, odd = <imath>5 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 = 125</imath>

Case 4: odd, odd, even = <imath>5 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 = 125</imath>

Simply sum up the cases to get your answer, <imath>100 + 100 + 125 + 125 = \boxed{\textbf{(D)~}450}</imath>.

- Wesseywes7254

==Solution 2 (Bijection)==
We will show that the answer is <imath>450</imath> by proving a bijection between the three digit integers that have an even number of even digits and the three digit integers that have an odd number of even digits. For every even number with an odd number of even digits, we increment the number's last digit by <imath>1</imath>, unless the last digit is <imath>9</imath>, in which case it becomes <imath>0</imath>. It is very easy to show that every number with an even number of even digits is mapped to every number with an odd number of even digits, and vice versa. Thus, the answer is half the number of three digit numbers, or <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)~}450}</imath>

~mathboy100

==Solution 3==
There are 9 possibilities for the first choice of a three-digit number in the hundreds place, excluding <imath>0</imath>. Now we have a few cases:

Case 1: The first digit is odd

In this case, only <imath>1</imath> even digit is permitted, since <imath>3</imath> is impossible. The even digit can be either in the tens or the ones, so we have <imath>5\cdot5\cdot2</imath> ways to place the even digit and odd digit.

Case 2: The first digit is even

In this case, either all digits can be even or the rest of the digits can be odd. That's <imath>5\cdot5</imath> for both of them, yielding <imath>5\cdot5\cdot2</imath> in total.

Thus, both cases result in multiplying the <imath>9</imath> by <imath>5\cdot5\cdot2</imath>, or <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)~}450}</imath>
